paragraphs: ACT addresses the cost of producing reliable training labels by giving language models two jobs: proposing annotations and judging which annotations may be wrong. Human reviewers then concentrate on the cases flagged as suspicious. The approach uses model judgment to direct limited human attention toward examples that appear to need it most.

Using multimodal language models lets the pipeline cover text, images, and tasks involving both. The authors also derive seven empirical insights about improving annotation quality while reducing human effort, translating those findings into practical guidelines. Beyond the labeling workflow, they theoretically examine modifications to the training loss that can help models trained on ACT annotations perform similarly to models trained on entirely human-labeled data.

In the reported experiments, the performance gap falls below 2% on most benchmark datasets, with human costs reduced by up to 90%. These are qualified experimental results: the gap is reported for most datasets, and the cost reduction is an upper-end outcome. Together, they support targeted human review as a useful way to balance annotation expense and downstream model performance.
neurips-2025-act-as-human-multimodal-lar.tldr: ACT combines model-generated labels, model-based error detection, and targeted human review to reduce annotation costs while keeping downstream performance close to human-labeled training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether language models can learn strong gameplay in complex card games. The authors study eight games, focusing on supervised fine-tuning with high-quality gameplay examples. They examine both how well models learn individual games and whether one model can develop proficiency across several games while retaining its broader abilities.

The findings suggest that this training can bring language models close to strong game-playing AI systems. Learning multiple games together has mixed effects: games with similar rules can reinforce one another, whereas games with dissimilar rules can create conflicts. This makes the relationship between tasks relevant to how successfully a shared model learns them.

The study also finds a tradeoff between game specialization and general capability. Models lose some broader ability as they learn complex games, but adding a certain amount of general instruction data can mitigate that decline. The results support the versatility of supervised language-model training for gameplay, while showing that approaching strong game AI and preserving general abilities depend on how training data is combined.
neurips-2025-can-large-language-models-m.tldr: Supervised training can bring language models close to strong card-game AIs, with cross-game transfer and general capability retention depending on the training mix.

paragraphs: CADS treats the available training compute as part of deciding which data to use. The motivation is empirical: across changing budgets, existing selection methods do not consistently beat one another or even random selection. A useful subset therefore depends on the training resources available, alongside the quantity, quality, and distribution of its examples.

The method uses two linked optimization problems. An inner problem trains a model on selected data within the budget, while an outer problem adjusts the selection using model evaluation. To make this affordable, the authors estimate selection gradients without constructing a Hessian matrix. They also move the inner optimization requirement into a penalty in the outer objective, reducing a needed gradient calculation to estimating the minimum of a one-dimensional loss.

CADS-E selects individual examples, while CADS-S selects groups of examples by source for greater scalability. Experiments across vision and language benchmarks report gains of up to 14.42% over baselines. Compared with conventional implementations of the two-level optimization, CADS delivers 3–20 times faster execution, with larger budgets associated with greater acceleration.
neurips-2025-computational-budget-should.tldr: CADS selects training data jointly with compute constraints, reporting improved performance and faster optimization across vision and language benchmarks.

paragraphs: A diffusion model trained on equilibrium molecular configurations can generate samples and provide a learned score from which molecular forces can be derived. This paper examines a mismatch between those uses: ordinary diffusion sampling can recover the training distribution even when the forces implied by the same model produce an inconsistent energy-based interpretation.

The authors trace the problem to inaccurate scores at very small diffusion timesteps. In that regime, the learned model fails to obey the Fokker–Planck equation describing the relevant distributional evolution. They propose an energy-based diffusion model with a regularization term derived from that equation, making consistency between sampling and simulation an explicit training concern.

The approach is demonstrated through sampling and simulation of several biomolecular systems, including fast-folding proteins. The paper also introduces a transferable Boltzmann emulator for dipeptides, reporting improved consistency and efficient sampling while supporting simulation. The central contribution is connecting two uses of a learned molecular distribution that can otherwise disagree: drawing equilibrium configurations and deriving forces for molecular dynamics.
neurips-2025-consistent-sampling-and-sim.tldr: A Fokker–Planck-derived training penalty improves agreement between molecular diffusion sampling and simulations driven by the model’s learned forces.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical account of why training on intermediate reasoning steps can help a learner master functions that require several steps. Ordinary supervised examples reveal an input and its final answer. Chain-of-thought supervision adds intermediate information, giving the learner more evidence about which candidate explanations of the task fit the training data.

The key quantity, called CoT information, measures the extra ability of those intermediate steps to distinguish hypotheses with different overall input-to-output behavior. This focuses the analysis on how informative the reasoning supervision is for separating competing solutions. The theoretical benefit is therefore tied to the discrimination that the added steps provide.

The authors establish both upper bounds on learning requirements and information-theoretic lower bounds, expressed through CoT information. These results show how reasoning-step supervision can produce substantially faster learning rates than supervision using final answers alone. By characterizing both achievable rates and fundamental constraints through the same quantity, the work provides a framework for understanding when richer supervision can reduce the examples needed to learn.
neurips-2025-cot-information-improved-sa.tldr: The paper introduces CoT information to characterize how intermediate reasoning supervision can reduce the number of examples needed for learning.

paragraphs: This work focuses on the experience an agent gathers while learning to act in a high-dimensional environment. As the number of possible states grows, learning an effective policy becomes computationally challenging. The paper approaches that difficulty through the agent’s interactions with its environment, introducing a learning paradigm based on experiences obtained from counteractive actions.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis supporting efficient and accelerated learning under this paradigm. They also report that the approach adds no computational complexity while substantially accelerating training. This makes the way experience is obtained central to the proposed improvement: the contribution concerns the learning process during interaction, rather than only the final quality of the learned policy.

Experiments use the Arcade Learning Environment with high-dimensional state representations. The reported outcomes support the theoretical analysis, showing significant performance improvements and stronger sample efficiency in the evaluated environments. These findings suggest that counteractive-action experience can help agents learn more effectively from environmental interactions, while the stated evidence remains tied to the theoretical treatment and experimental settings studied.
neurips-2025-counteractive-rl-rethinking.tldr: Counteractive RL uses experiences from counteractive actions to improve training speed and sample efficiency without reported additional computational complexity.

paragraphs: DreamVLA connects forecasting the world with predicting robot actions. The paper argues that forecasting future images alone involves redundant information and does not adequately capture geometry, meaning, and spatial relationships. Its alternative predicts several kinds of world information to support inverse dynamics modeling: determining actions through the relationship between current and anticipated states.

A mechanism guided by dynamic regions forecasts visual, depth, geometric, semantic, and segmentation cues. These cues form a compact representation intended to retain information relevant to action planning. A diffusion-based transformer then models the conditional distribution of future actions, separating action representations from shared latent features and accounting for multiple possible action outcomes.

The resulting framework establishes a loop between action prediction and world forecasting for manipulation tasks. Experiments cover both real robots and simulation, reporting a 76.7% success rate on real robot tasks and an average length of 4.45 on CALVIN ABC-D. These results demonstrate the approach in both settings, with the two reported measures describing different evaluations rather than a single combined performance score.
neurips-2025-dreamvla-a-vision-language-.tldr: DreamVLA forecasts multiple forms of world information and uses diffusion-based action prediction to guide robot manipulation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Frank–Wolfe optimization algorithm that incorporates corrective steps within a framework encompassing several existing variants. The authors establish tight convergence guarantees and an optimal face identification property. The latter concerns identifying the part of the feasible region that contains an optimum, connecting the algorithm’s progress to the geometry of the optimization problem.

For convex quadratic objectives, they propose two efficient ways to perform corrections: one based on linear optimization and another based on solving linear systems. Under suitable conditions, they prove finite-time convergence. That qualification matters because the finite-time result is attached to conditions on the setting, rather than asserted for every problem handled by the framework.

The benefits also extend to methods that solve quadratic subproblems inside a larger optimization process. The authors improve convergence rates for Split Conditional Gradient and establish broader applicability for Second-Order Conditional Gradient Sliding. Computational experiments show substantial speedups across the studied problem classes, supporting quadratic correction as both a theoretically useful and practically effective component.
neurips-2025-efficient-quadratic-correct.tldr: Efficient quadratic correction steps strengthen convergence guarantees and accelerate Frank–Wolfe methods across the studied optimization problems.

paragraphs: SnapViT addresses the mismatch between a few available sizes of pretrained vision models and the many compute budgets encountered in deployment. It creates pruned Vision Transformers whose inference cost can be adjusted across a continuum of budgets. This adaptation takes place after pretraining and requires neither model retraining nor labeled examples.

The pruning strategy combines gradient information with correlations among structures throughout the network. An evolutionary algorithm approximates off-diagonal Hessian structure, allowing the method to account for relationships between components when deciding their importance. A self-supervised scoring mechanism also lets it operate on models that lack a classification head, broadening the range of pretrained models it can adapt.

Experiments on DINO, SigLIPv2, DeIT, and AugReg report stronger performance than state-of-the-art pruning methods across different sparsity levels. Generating the elastic models takes less than five minutes on one A100 GPU in the reported evaluation. The practical contribution is a relatively quick conversion from a fixed pretrained model into one adjustable to deployment compute constraints.
neurips-2025-elastic-vits-from-pretraine.tldr: SnapViT converts pretrained Vision Transformers into adjustable-compute models through structured pruning without labels or retraining.

paragraphs: Generative distribution embeddings extend the autoencoder idea from individual examples to whole distributions. An encoder receives a set of samples, and a conditional generator attempts to reproduce the distribution represented by that set. This allows a learned representation to describe a population of observations, supporting problems that require reasoning across multiple scales.

The framework combines generators with encoders satisfying a criterion called distributional invariance. The authors show that the resulting representations learn predictive sufficient statistics in Wasserstein space. For Gaussian and Gaussian mixture distributions, distances between latent representations approximately recover W2 distances, while interpolation approximately follows optimal transport trajectories. These are approximate geometric relationships for the stated distribution families.

Synthetic benchmarks show consistently stronger performance than the compared approaches. The paper also applies the framework to six computational biology problems, spanning donor representations, clonal dynamics, cellular perturbations, promoter design, and viral sequence modeling. These applications connect population-level representation learning to datasets of cells, images, and sequences, showing how the same distribution-based framework can support several forms of biological analysis.
neurips-2025-generative-distribution-emb.tldr: Generative distribution embeddings encode sample populations and reconstruct their distributions, supporting multiscale learning and approximate transport geometry.

paragraphs: KSP addresses calibration in survival models: how well their predicted probabilities agree with observed outcomes over time. The paper focuses on adjusting predictions after a model has been trained. Its motivation is that existing calibration approaches often depend on heuristic bins or additional nonparametric estimates, making continuous-time predictions and complex model outputs harder to handle flexibly.

The proposed post-processing framework uses the Kolmogorov–Smirnov metric as its basis. It avoids both discretizing predictions and estimating a Kaplan–Meier curve. Removing those dependencies gives the method a streamlined design intended to work across different survival models. The authors also analyze the metric theoretically and discuss extending the approach to calibration performed during model training.

Experiments span diverse real-world datasets and multiple survival models. Within these evaluations, KSP consistently improves calibration over existing methods while maintaining high predictive accuracy. The findings indicate that adjusting probability reliability need not come with a loss of strong predictive performance in the tested settings, and that the framework can be used across varied model choices.
neurips-2025-ksp-kolmogorov-smirnov-metr.tldr: KSP improves survival-model calibration through KS-based post-processing without discretization or Kaplan–Meier estimation.

paragraphs: The paper examines a hidden shortcut in completing partial 3D shapes: training scans are often aligned to a standard frame. That alignment supplies pose and scale clues that networks can exploit by memorizing absolute positions. When real scans lack those clues, the resulting models can perform poorly despite appearing effective under aligned evaluation.

The proposed network builds in equivariance to SIM(3), covering changes in position, orientation, and scale. Its layers successively canonicalize features, reason about geometry invariant to those transformations, and restore the original frame. This organizes shape reasoning around intrinsic geometry while keeping the completed output consistent with the input’s coordinate frame.

Under an evaluation protocol that removes alignment shortcuts, the model outperforms both equivariant and augmentation baselines on PCN. It also reports a 17% reduction in minimal matching distance on KITTI and a 14% reduction in Chamfer distance ℓ1 on OmniObject3D. Performance under the stricter protocol even exceeds competitors evaluated with the hidden cues, supporting SIM(3) equivariance as an effective route to stronger generalization.
neurips-2025-learning-generalizable-shap.tldr: A SIM(3)-equivariant network improves shape completion by making its predictions consistent across changes in pose and scale.

paragraphs: Learning to Focus addresses distracting context that can pull a language model away from information needed to answer an instruction. Preliminary experiments show that removing certain distracting patterns improves reasoning accuracy and generation quality. The authors attribute this behavior to spurious training correlations that interfere with learning the causal relationship between instructions and responses.

The framework, called LeaF, has two stages. First, gradient-based comparisons with an advanced teacher model identify tokens treated as confounders in the training corpus. Second, those tokens are pruned during distillation. This removal acts as an intervention, while the student is trained to align its attention with the teacher’s distribution of focus over critical context.

Experiments report improvements on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and multi-hop question answering benchmarks. The trained model also pays less attention to confounding tokens at inference time. These results support the proposed link between intervening on distracting training tokens and improving later reasoning behavior, while the paper’s causal explanation remains the authors’ account of the observed phenomenon.
neurips-2025-learning-to-focus-causal-at.tldr: LeaF identifies distracting training tokens with teacher-guided gradients and prunes them during distillation to improve attention and reasoning.

paragraphs: T2MIR improves reinforcement-learning agents that adapt to downstream tasks through prompt conditioning. Such models must interpret several kinds of information—states, actions, and rewards—while handling tasks with different decision requirements. The paper treats these as two distinct sources of diversity and introduces separate mixture-of-experts components to address them within a transformer decision model.

The token-wise component specializes in the meanings of different input modalities. The task-wise component directs tasks to specialized experts, aiming to reduce conflicts between their training gradients. Both operate in parallel in place of the usual feedforward layer, and their outputs are concatenated before passing onward. A contrastive learning objective encourages the task router’s representation to retain information relevant to task identity.

Experiments report improved in-context learning capacity and stronger performance than several types of baselines. The architectural contribution is the explicit combination of specialization by token and specialization by task. This gives the shared decision model separate mechanisms for interpreting heterogeneous experience and accommodating a broad distribution of decision problems.
neurips-2025-mixture-of-experts-meets-in.tldr: T2MIR combines token-wise and task-wise expert routing to improve prompt-based adaptation in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how structural knowledge can transfer between graphs whose geometry does not fit a shared ordinary coordinate space. It proposes topological primitives as transferable units of structural meaning. The resulting G²SN-Transfer framework addresses representation, transfer, and evaluation together, creating a way to relate graph structure to aligned textual information.

TopoGraph-Mapping converts graphs into sequences using dictionaries of topological primitive distributions. G²SN then learns aligned text and topology representations through a dual-stream architecture and contrastive alignment. Its sequence model is driven by ordinary differential equations, with a convergence guarantee established theoretically. AdaCross-Transfer uses data-adaptive cross-attention to transfer knowledge in both full-parameter and parameter-frozen settings.

The authors introduce STA-18, pairing topological primitives with text across 18 graph datasets. Evaluations report state-of-the-art results on four structural learning tasks, averaging a 3.2% F1-score improvement. Transfer produces consistent improvements across 13 downstream tasks, averaging 5.2% gains. These results support the proposed structural units as useful carriers of knowledge across the evaluated graphs and tasks.
neurips-2025-one-for-all-universal-topol.tldr: G²SN-Transfer represents graphs through topological primitives aligned with text to improve structural learning and cross-graph transfer.

paragraphs: FedAux addresses federated learning when different clients hold different subgraphs of a larger graph. Their local data distributions can differ substantially, creating a need to share useful knowledge while retaining client-specific behavior. The framework learns how to compare and combine local models without exchanging raw data or node embeddings.

Each client trains a graph neural network together with an auxiliary projection vector that maps node embeddings into one dimension. Soft sorting and a lightweight one-dimensional convolution refine this ordered representation, helping the projection capture information specific to the client. After training, the projection vectors act as compact signatures that the server uses to estimate similarities between clients.

Those similarities determine how model parameters are mixed, producing personalized models while retaining cross-client knowledge transfer. The authors provide theoretical analysis of convergence and the rationale for the design. Across diverse graph benchmarks, FedAux substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines in accuracy and personalization. The main contribution is a learned client-comparison mechanism that guides selective sharing under heterogeneous graph data.
neurips-2025-personalized-subgraph-feder.tldr: FedAux learns compact client signatures to guide personalized model sharing across heterogeneous subgraphs without sharing raw data or node embeddings.

paragraphs: Inverse folding seeks amino acid sequences that will form a desired three-dimensional protein structure. This paper improves an inverse-folding model using feedback from a separate protein-folding model. The training signal comes from comparing the predicted structures of candidate sequences with the target structure, connecting sequence generation to its intended structural outcome.

For each target, the inverse-folding model samples candidates, and the folding model predicts their structures. Structural comparisons then produce pairwise preference labels. Direct Preference Optimization uses those labels to fine-tune the sequence generator toward preferred candidates. This turns structure feedback into a training objective through relative preferences between generated sequences.

On the CATH 4.2 test set, fine-tuning improves sequence recovery and raises average TM-Score from 0.77 to 0.81, indicating greater structural similarity. Repeating the procedure on challenging structures produces a reported 79.5% average TM-Score increase relative to the baseline model. These findings support preference optimization as a promising way to improve sequence design using predicted structural feedback.
neurips-2025-protein-inverse-folding-fro.tldr: Preference optimization uses folding-model feedback to improve generated protein sequences’ similarity to desired structures.

paragraphs: Rig3R reconstructs scenes and estimates motion from images captured by multi-camera rigs. Its motivation is that treating images as an unstructured collection overlooks relationships among synchronized cameras. The model incorporates available metadata, such as camera identity, time, and rig poses, while also learning to infer rig structure when that information is missing.

It jointly predicts pointmaps and two kinds of raymaps. Global-frame pose raymaps support reasoning about the agent’s motion. Rig-centered raymaps describe camera relationships in a coordinate frame consistent across time, enabling rig discovery directly from images. These outputs connect scene geometry, global motion, and the organization of cameras within a shared learned representation.

Across diverse real-world rig datasets, the paper reports state-of-the-art results for 3D reconstruction, camera pose estimation, and rig discovery. It reports improvements of 17–45% mAA over traditional and learned methods. All predictions are produced in one forward pass, without post-processing or iterative refinement, showing that explicitly representing rig relationships can support several related estimation tasks within one model.
neurips-2025-rig3r-rig-aware-conditionin.tldr: Rig3R uses or infers multi-camera rig structure to jointly reconstruct scenes, estimate poses, and discover camera arrangements in one forward pass.

paragraphs: SALMONN-omni aims to support fluid spoken conversation through a single full-duplex speech language model. Existing modular systems can accumulate errors across components responsible for detecting speech, interruptions, or conversation state. The proposed model handles conversation without injecting audio codecs into its token space, addressing another design choice associated with degraded speech performance in prior approaches.

A dynamic thinking mechanism inside the language-model backbone learns when to move between speaking and listening states. This places conversational timing within the model itself. The evaluation includes turn-taking, brief listener responses, echo cancellation, and interruptions whose appropriateness depends on context, connecting the architecture to demands of natural spoken interaction.

On spoken question answering and open-domain dialogue benchmarks, SALMONN-omni reports at least 30% relative improvement over existing open-source full-duplex models. It is also highly competitive with half-duplex and turn-based systems despite using substantially less training data. Reinforcement learning further improves performance in complex conversational scenarios, supporting the standalone approach across both content-oriented benchmarks and interaction behaviors.
neurips-2025-salmonn-omni-a-standalone-s.tldr: SALMONN-omni uses a standalone speech model with learned speaking–listening transitions to improve full-duplex conversation without codec tokens.

paragraphs: Computer-use grounding connects a natural-language instruction to the relevant interface action. This paper argues that short referring expressions underrepresent the demands of real software use, which also involves understanding layouts, recognizing elements, and manipulating them precisely. It introduces OSWorld-G, a benchmark of 564 carefully annotated samples spanning these different task types.

The authors also create Jedi, a dataset containing four million grounding examples synthesized through task decomposition from multiple perspectives. Models of several sizes trained on Jedi outperform existing approaches on ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G. This links the data-generation strategy to improved performance across multiple grounding evaluations.

The study then examines whether better grounding improves complete computer tasks. It reports an increase from 23% to 51% on OSWorld, reaching state-of-the-art performance in the evaluated setup. Ablations identify factors affecting grounding and show that combining specialized data for different interface elements supports compositional generalization to unfamiliar interfaces. The contribution therefore spans both locating actions and improving broader agent behavior.
neurips-2025-scaling-computer-use-ground.tldr: A richer interface-grounding benchmark and four-million-example synthetic dataset improve both grounding models and complete computer-use task performance.

paragraphs: Comparing neural recordings with computational models is difficult when only a limited number of neurons can be recorded at once. This paper studies how that sampling constraint affects two representational similarity measures, CKA and CCA. The goal is to distinguish the similarity of the underlying representations from distortions introduced by observing only a subset of neurons.

Using random matrix theory, the authors relate measured similarity to spectral properties of the representations. They show that finite neuron sampling systematically underestimates similarity, with eigenvector delocalization identified as the main cause. The analysis therefore explains a directional measurement bias, rather than treating small samples solely as a source of uncertain estimates.

The authors introduce a denoising method to infer population-level similarity from limited recordings. Predictions from the theory are validated on synthetic and real datasets, and the method enables accurate analysis with small neuron samples in the studied settings. This provides a way to interpret low observed similarity more carefully when recording constraints distort the comparison.
neurips-2025-spectral-analysis-of-repres.tldr: Random matrix analysis explains why limited neuron samples underestimate representational similarity and motivates a population-level denoising method.

paragraphs: This paper explores using squared families of probability distributions to express prior beliefs in Bayesian inference. These families have more commonly served as likelihoods, describing how observations arise. The authors investigate their role on the other side of the Bayesian update, asking whether they can support useful and computationally manageable prior distributions.

They find that squared families can form conjugate families, often making inference and marginal likelihood calculations tractable or available in closed form. The application is Bayesian regression over features learned by a neural network, with feature learning performed end to end. This produces a rich, multimodal alternative to Gaussian processes using neural features, a setting commonly called deep kernel learning.

The method is demonstrated on few-shot learning, where the authors report outperforming existing neural approaches based on Gaussian processes and normalizing flows. The significance is the combination of richer distributions with manageable Bayesian calculations. The abstract qualifies that computational advantage as occurring often, so the result supports useful conjugate constructions without implying every squared-family prior yields closed-form inference.
neurips-2025-squared-families-are-useful.tldr: Squared probability families can provide tractable conjugate priors and a multimodal Bayesian regression alternative that performs well in few-shot learning.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether flat regions of a training loss reliably indicate good generalization in two-layer, overparameterized ReLU networks with multivariate inputs. Its theory covers both generalization gaps for flat solutions and mean-squared error in function estimation using stable minima. This extends the analysis beyond earlier work requiring interpolation or restricting inputs to one dimension.

Upper and lower bounds show that flatness does imply generalization in the studied settings, but the convergence rates necessarily deteriorate exponentially as input dimension increases. The authors contrast this with known behavior of low-norm solutions associated with weight decay. Their result identifies a substantial distinction between controlling loss curvature and controlling weight magnitude.

The lower-bound construction reveals a mechanism called neural shattering: neurons can activate rarely while carrying large weights, allowing flat solutions to perform poorly in high dimensions. Numerical simulations corroborate the theoretical findings. The conclusion is specific to the analyzed network and estimation settings, explaining why flatness alone can offer weak generalization guarantees as dimensionality grows.
neurips-2025-stable-minima-of-relu-neura.tldr: For the studied two-layer ReLU networks, flatness-based generalization rates worsen exponentially with input dimension, unlike known low-norm guarantees.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can sample several tokens in parallel, suggesting a possible speed advantage over autoregressive generation. Yet the authors observe that current open-source models need enough steps to match accuracy on representative tasks that their inference costs can be higher. The paper asks whether this reflects a fundamental constraint by analyzing masked diffusion models.

The answer depends strongly on the evaluation metric. Under mild conditions, the theory shows that near-optimal perplexity can be achieved with a constant number of sampling steps, independent of sequence length. This establishes a possible efficiency benefit under that objective, rather than a claim that current implementations already realize it.

For low sequence error rates, the worst-case result changes: the required number of steps must grow linearly with sequence length. That removes the step-count advantage when correctness of the complete sequence is demanding, as can matter for reasoning chains. The analysis explains why favorable results under perplexity do not automatically establish an efficiency advantage under whole-sequence correctness.
neurips-2025-theoretical-benefit-and-lim.tldr: Masked diffusion can reach near-optimal perplexity in constant steps under mild conditions, but low sequence error requires linearly many steps in the worst case.

paragraphs: This paper addresses two challenges in learned job scheduling: restricted exploration when training one decision-maker and the effort required to design rewards for different scheduling variants. Its framework optimizes several policies that share a single neural network and a common objective, while allowing each policy to develop a specialized strategy.

Training is fully self-supervised and does not require reward functions. The method also adjusts how strongly the model imitates its self-generated labels according to their quality. This links the strength of the learning signal to the reliability of the guidance available, while the multiple policies provide diverse approaches to the same scheduling objective.

Experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning methods across six job-scheduling variants. The approach also performs strongly on other combinatorial optimization problems, providing evidence of usefulness beyond scheduling. The contribution combines policy diversity with self-supervised optimization, addressing both how broadly the model explores solutions and how it obtains training guidance across different problem variants.
neurips-2025-towards-generalizable-multi.tldr: A self-supervised framework trains diverse scheduling policies in one network without reward functions and outperforms RL methods across six scheduling variants.
